CHAPTER 1.6 · LEARNING AREA 1

CHAPTER 1.6 · LEARNING AREA 1 · JANUARY

Parabolas made to measure

A jet of water is to land exactly in the pool, an arch is to pass through three given points, a line is only to touch a parabola. Now you turn the tables: from conditions you make an equation of a function. And you learn to deal with parameters, where the result depends on which number you substitute.

6 LESSONS2 UNITSGRAPHING CALCULATOR WITHOUT CASCASE ANALYSIS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • write and read quadratic functions in factorised form
  • set up equations of functions from given conditions: choose the suitable form
  • solve systems of equations with three unknowns on the graphing calculator
  • investigate families of functions and carry out a case analysis according to the parameter
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

What is the positive zero of $f(x) = x^2 - 4$?

$x = 2$ (and $x = -2$)

What is the discriminant $\left(\tfrac{p}{2}\right)^2 - q$ of $x^2 - 6x + 9 = 0$?

$9 - 9 = 0$

What is $(x - 2)(x + 3)$?

$x^2 + 3x - 2x - 6$

Solve $a + b = 4$, $a - b = 2$. What is $a$?

Add: $2a = 6$

EXPLORATIONSTO GET STARTED · IN GROUPS
THE FOUNTAIN

A jet of water hits the surface of the water 1 m and 5 m from the edge of the pool. Halfway between, it is 2 m high.

  • Sketch the jet in a coordinate system. Which points do you know?
  • Find an equation. Which form of the equation of a parabola is the most convenient?
→ Unit 1
THREE POINTS, ONE PARABOLA

Draw three points that do not lie on a straight line, for example $(0, 1)$, $(1, 0)$ and $(3, 7)$.

  • Is there always exactly one parabola through them? What happens if two points lie one above the other?
→ Unit 1
TOUCH, CUT, MISS

Draw the standard parabola $y = x^2$ and the lines $y = 2x + c$ for $c = 1$, $c = 0$, $c = -1$ and $c = -2$.

  • How many common points are there in each case?
  • For which $c$ does the line only touch the parabola?

UNIT 13 LESSONS

1Linear factors and equations of functions from conditions

The fountain has the zeros $x = 1$ and $x = 5$. So $f(x) = a(x - 1)(x - 5)$ fits: for every $a$ the term vanishes exactly there. The point $(3, 2)$ fixes $a$: $a \cdot 2 \cdot (-2) = 2$, so $a = -0.5$ and $f(x) = -0.5(x - 1)(x - 5)$.

A quadratic function has three coefficients. That is why you need three conditions to fix it. If you choose wisely which form to start with, you save a lot of calculation: a known vertex puts two conditions into the vertex form, two zeros put two into the factorised form.

KEY POINT · FACTORISED FORM AND CONDITIONS

Factorised form: $f(x) = a(x - x_1)(x - x_2)$ with the zeros $x_1$, $x_2$. For a double zero $f(x) = a(x - x_1)^2$. Without a zero there is no factorisation into linear factors.

Choose the suitable form: vertex known → $a(x - d)^2 + e$ · zeros known → $a(x - x_1)(x - x_2)$ · any three points → $ax^2 + bx + c$.

Three points substituted into $ax^2 + bx + c$ give a system of equations with three unknowns $a$, $b$, $c$. Larger systems are solved on the graphing calculator.

Factoring out helps: $2x^2 - 4x - 6 = 2(x^2 - 2x - 3) = 2(x - 3)(x + 1)$.

A point on the $y$-axis gives $c$ at once: $f(0) = c$.

INTERACTIVE · PARABOLA THROUGH THREE POINTS

Drag the three points. The system of equations for $a$, $b$, $c$ and its solution appear below.

WITH THE GRAPHING CALCULATOR · SYSTEM OF EQUATIONS WITH THREE UNKNOWNS

Enter the coefficients as an augmented matrix, so for $(0, 1)$, $(1, 0)$, $(3, 7)$ the rows $0\;0\;1\;|\;1$, $\;1\;1\;1\;|\;0$, $\;9\;3\;1\;|\;7$. Then call the equation solver or the function “rref” (reduced row echelon form). The last column shows $a = 1.5$, $b = -2.5$, $c = 1$.

EXAMPLE 1 · FACTORISING INTO LINEAR FACTORS

Write $f(x) = 2x^2 - 4x - 6$ in factorised form.

Factor out $2$: $2(x^2 - 2x - 3)$. Zeros of $x^2 - 2x - 3$: $x = 1 \pm 2$, so $3$ and $-1$.

$f(x) = 2(x - 3)(x + 1)$

EXAMPLE 2 · THREE POINTS

Determine the parabola through $A(0, 1)$, $B(1, 0)$ and $C(3, 7)$.

$A$: $c = 1$. $B$: $a + b + 1 = 0$. $C$: $9a + 3b + 1 = 7$, so $3a + b = 2$.

Subtract: $2a = 3$, $a = 1.5$, $b = -2.5$. $f(x) = 1.5x^2 - 2.5x + 1$

EXERCISES

Write in factorised form, if possible: a) $x^2 - 5x + 6$   b) $2x^2 - 8$   c) $-x^2 + 2x - 1$   d) $x^2 + 4$

a) $(x - 2)(x - 3)$   b) $2(x - 2)(x + 2)$   c) $-(x - 1)^2$   d) not possible, no zero

A parabola has the zeros $-2$ and $4$ and passes through $(0, -4)$. Determine its equation.

$f(x) = a(x + 2)(x - 4)$, $f(0) = -8a = -4$, so $a = 0.5$: $f(x) = 0.5(x + 2)(x - 4)$

A parabola has the vertex $S(2, -1)$ and passes through $P(4, 3)$. Determine its equation in general form.

$a(x - 2)^2 - 1$ with $4a - 1 = 3$: $a = 1$. $f(x) = (x - 2)^2 - 1 = x^2 - 4x + 3$

Determine the parabola through $(-1, 6)$, $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 3)$, without and with the graphing calculator.

Subtract the first two equations from each other; then $a$ and $c$ drop out.

$a - b + c = 6$, $a + b + c = 2$, $4a + 2b + c = 3$. First $b = -2$, then $a + c = 4$ and $4a + c = 7$: $a = 1$, $c = 3$. $f(x) = x^2 - 2x + 3$

The nozzle of a fountain is 0.5 m above the water. 2 m further on, the jet reaches its highest point at a height of 2.5 m. How far from the nozzle does it hit the water?

$f(x) = a(x - 2)^2 + 2.5$ with $f(0) = 4a + 2.5 = 0.5$: $a = -0.5$. $f(x) = 0 \Rightarrow (x - 2)^2 = 5 \Rightarrow x = 2 + \sqrt5 \approx$ 4.24 m.

TEST YOURSELF!

$f(x) = a(x - 1)(x - 5)$ passes through $(3, 2)$. What is $a$?

$-4a = 2$, $a = -0.5$

Which term can not be factorised into linear factors?

$x^2 + 9 = 0$ has no solution.

What is the coefficient $a$ of the parabola through $(0, 1)$, $(1, 0)$ and $(3, 7)$?

$a = 1.5$

UNIT 23 LESSONS

2Families of functions and case analysis

When does the line $y = 2x + c$ meet the parabola $y = x^2$? Setting them equal gives $x^2 - 2x - c = 0$ with the discriminant $D = 1 + c$. For $c > -1$ there are two points of intersection, for $c = -1$ exactly one (the line then touches the parabola), and for $c < -1$ none.

If a term contains a parameter, it does not describe one function but a whole family. Questions such as “How many zeros?” then have no single answer, but one answer for each range of the parameter. These ranges are set out in a case analysis.

KEY POINT · FAMILY OF FUNCTIONS AND CASE ANALYSIS

A family of functions $f_a$ is a function term with a parameter $a$. Every number for $a$ gives one function of the family.

If a result depends on the parameter, you investigate the cases separately. Typical reasons:

· the sign of the discriminant ($D > 0$, $D = 0$, $D < 0$) · a division by a term containing the parameter (may it be zero?) · the parameter stands in front of $x^2$: for the value zero it is no longer a parabola.

Always consider the boundary cases such as $D = 0$ separately.

Tip: first collect the cases, then solve each one separately and at the end write an overview of all the cases.

Locus: the vertices of a family often lie on a curve themselves. For $x^2 + ax$ it is the parabola $y = -x^2$.

INTERACTIVE · THREE FAMILIES OF FUNCTIONS

Grey: the members for integer parameters. Yellow: the member for the slider. The table shows which case you are in.

EXAMPLE 3 · NUMBER OF ZEROS

Investigate the zeros of $f_a(x) = x^2 - 2x + a$.

$x^2 - 2x + a = 0$: $x = 1 \pm \sqrt{1 - a}$, the discriminant is $D = 1 - a$.

$a < 1$: two zeros · $a = 1$: one, $x = 1$ · $a > 1$: none

EXAMPLE 4 · THE PARAMETER IN FRONT OF $x^2$

How many solutions does $k\,x^2 + 4x + 2 = 0$ have, depending on $k$?

$k = 0$: what remains is $4x + 2 = 0$, exactly one solution $x = -0.5$.

$k \neq 0$: divide by $k$, $D = \tfrac{4}{k^2} - \tfrac{2}{k} = \tfrac{4 - 2k}{k^2}$. Two solutions for $k < 2$ ($k \neq 0$), one for $k = 2$, none for $k > 2$.

EXERCISES

For which $a$ does $f_a(x) = x^2 + a$ have two zeros, exactly one or none?

$a < 0$: two ($\pm\sqrt{-a}$) · $a = 0$: one ($x = 0$) · $a > 0$: none

For which $a$ does $f_a(x) = a\,x^2 + 3$ pass through $P(2, -5)$?

$4a + 3 = -5 \Rightarrow a = -2$

For which $c$ does the line $y = 2x + c$ touch the standard parabola? At which point?

$D = 1 + c = 0 \Rightarrow c = -1$. Then $x^2 - 2x + 1 = (x - 1)^2 = 0$: point of contact $(1, 1)$.

Carry out a case analysis for the number of zeros of $f_t(x) = x^2 - t\,x + 4$.

$D = \tfrac{t^2}{4} - 4$. Two zeros for $t < -4$ or $t > 4$, one for $t = \pm 4$, none for $-4 < t < 4$.

Show: the vertices of the parabolas $f_a(x) = x^2 + a\,x$ all lie on the curve $y = -x^2$.

Completing the square: $f_a(x) = \left(x + \tfrac{a}{2}\right)^2 - \tfrac{a^2}{4}$, so $S\left(-\tfrac{a}{2}, -\tfrac{a^2}{4}\right)$. With $x = -\tfrac{a}{2}$ we have $a = -2x$ and $y = -\tfrac{4x^2}{4} = -x^2$.

TEST YOURSELF!

For which $a$ does $x^2 - 2x + a$ have exactly one zero?

$D = 1 - a = 0$

For which $c$ does $y = 2x + c$ touch the parabola $y = x^2$?

$c = -1$

How many zeros does $f_a(x) = x^2 + a$ have for $a = -4$?

$x^2 = 4$: $\pm 2$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Read off the zeros and the opening of $f(x) = -2(x + 3)(x - 1)$. Where is the vertex?

Zeros $-3$ and $1$, opens downwards. Vertex halfway between at $x = -1$: $f(-1) = -2 \cdot 2 \cdot (-2) = 8$, so $S(-1, 8)$.

A parabola $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$ cuts the $y$-axis at 3 and has the vertex $S(2, -1)$. Determine $a$, $b$, $c$ in two ways.

Vertex form: $a(x - 2)^2 - 1$ with $f(0) = 4a - 1 = 3$, so $a = 1$: $x^2 - 4x + 3$. Or with equations: $c = 3$, symmetry $b = -4a$, $f(2) = -1$.

Connecting with chapter 1.4: for which $a$ does the system of equations $y = x^2$, $y = a$ have two solutions, one or none? Interpret graphically.

$x^2 = a$: two solutions for $a > 0$, one for $a = 0$, none for $a < 0$. The horizontal line $y = a$ cuts, touches or misses the parabola.

For which $a$ does $a\,x^2 - 2x + 1 = 0$ have exactly two solutions? Pay attention to the case $a = 0$.

$a = 0$: $-2x + 1 = 0$, only one solution. $a \neq 0$: $D = \tfrac{1}{a^2} - \tfrac{1}{a} = \tfrac{1 - a}{a^2} > 0$ for $a < 1$. So exactly two solutions for $a < 1$ with $a \neq 0$.

EXCURSIONA MISTAKE WITH CONSEQUENCES

Chain or parabola?

If you hang a chain from two points, it looks like a parabola. In 1638 Galileo Galilei thought it was one. Only in 1691 did Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Christiaan Huygens and Johann Bernoulli show independently of each other: the curve is a different one, the catenary. Near the lowest point the two hardly differ, but further out they do.

For a suspension bridge, on the other hand, the parabola is very accurate: there the cable mainly carries the evenly distributed roadway, not its own weight. Under this load it takes on exactly the shape of a parabola.

Sources: Galileo Galilei, “Discorsi e dimostrazioni matematiche intorno a due nuove scienze” (1638), second day. · The solutions of Leibniz, Huygens and Johann Bernoulli appeared in June 1691 in the “Acta Eruditorum” (Leipzig).

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

FACTORISED FORM

$a(x - x_1)(x - x_2)$: zeros can be read off directly. Without zeros, no factorisation.

$2x^2 - 4x - 6 = 2(x - 3)(x + 1)$

SUITABLE FORM

Vertex → vertex form · zeros → factorised form · three points → general form with a system of equations

Fountain: $-0.5(x - 1)(x - 5)$

THREE POINTS

Substitute into $ax^2 + bx + c$, three equations, solve on the graphing calculator.

$(0, 1)$, $(1, 0)$, $(3, 7)$: $1.5x^2 - 2.5x + 1$

FAMILY OF FUNCTIONS

A term with a parameter describes many functions.

$f_a(x) = x^2 - 2x + a$

CASE ANALYSIS

Discriminant, division by parameter terms, parameter in front of $x^2$ — boundary cases separately.

$a < 1$: two · $a = 1$: one · $a > 1$: no zeros
